title: The tables go over (Matthew 21:12–13)
hookLine: in the temple courts he overturns the money changers' tables

cards: Children taken up in his arms. Hands on the sick. A king on a donkey.
And then this. The temple in Jerusalem, days before Passover: the center of Jewish worship, packed with pilgrims from everywhere.
The outer court, a huge open space, is full of stalls: people selling doves and animals for the sacrifices, money changers at their tables. Noise, bargaining, animals, crowds. And Jesus walks in.

teach.b: Matthew tells it fast, in the King James Bible: "And Jesus went into the temple of God, and cast out all them that sold and bought in the temple, and overthrew the tables of the moneychangers, and the seats of them that sold doves."
Coins spilling across the stones. Birds flapping.

teach.h: A HOUSE OF PRAYER FOR ALL NATIONS.
teach.b: Then he explains, quoting two prophets at once: "It is written, My house shall be called the house of prayer; but ye have made it a den of thieves."
The first half is from Isaiah; Mark gives the full line: a house of prayer for all nations.

The second half is from Jeremiah, who stood in the gate of the temple of his own day and warned people not to treat God's house as a den, a hideout. So this isn't an attack on the temple, or on Judaism.
It's a Jewish prophet in the line of Isaiah and Jeremiah, calling the temple back to what it was for.
The selling itself served a purpose: pilgrims from far away needed doves and animals to offer, and someone to change their money.
But some readers point out that the stalls likely stood in the outer court, where people who weren't Jewish could come and pray. If that court is a market, where do they go?
All four Gospels tell this story; John puts it near the start of Jesus's work, and adds a whip of cords. And look at what Matthew says happens right after the tables go over.

teach.h: THEN THE BLIND AND THE LAME COME.
teach.b: The blind and the lame come to him in the temple, and he heals them, and children start shouting hosanna.

teach.h: MY HOUSE SHALL BE CALLED THE HOUSE OF PRAYER.
teach.b: The noise of trade gives way to the noise of healing and praise.

how: Many churches read the cleansing of the temple in Lent or Holy Week. Christians often turn to it when thinking about keeping places of worship for prayer, and about money and faith.

games.q: you're a pilgrim in the outer court. you've come to pray, but the court is full of stalls and bargaining. a teacher starts overturning the tables. what happens next, in Matthew?
o: the temple guards arrest him on the spot.
the blind and the lame come to him, and he heals them.
games.why: the blind and the lame come to him in the temple, and he heals them, and children cry hosanna.

practice: Think of one cluttered corner in your life: a desk, a shelf, a car seat, a phone's home screen, or a crowded hour with no room left in it. Picture it clear, with room to breathe, room to think, room to pray if you pray.
You don't have to clear it all; just choose the one small table you'd turn over first.

wordCard.voice: Moneychangers. The traders Jesus found at their tables in the temple's outer court, and sent scattering so the court could be, again, a house of prayer.

orig.note: Greek: a money changer, from kollybos, a small coin or the fee for changing money.

carryVoice: Your line: make room for prayer. Tomorrow, a supper in Bethany, and a jar of perfume. See you then.
